hero.title: Understand the pattern. Try a different response.
hero.summary: CBT connects what happens, how you interpret it, how you feel, and what you do next. Learn the model, see a worked example, and understand what the work can involve.

panel.title: Curiosity before conclusions.
panel.text: CBT is not simply positive thinking. It is a structured way to investigate patterns and practice more useful responses.

items.title: Understand the model
items.text: Thoughts, feelings, physical responses, and actions.

items.title: Look inside a session
items.text: A collaborative process, not a worksheet assembly line.

sections.title: The event is one part of the story.
paragraphs: Cognitive behavioral therapy examines relationships between interpretations, feelings, and behavior. A situation matters, and so does the meaning attached to it. CBT uses an individualized understanding of these patterns to organize treatment rather than assuming every person has the same problem.

Cognitive work looks at thinking: what went through your mind, what supports it, and whether another interpretation fits the information. Behavioral work looks at what you do: habits, avoidance, routines, or actions that could provide new learning. Neither side requires dismissing a genuine difficulty.

The model is useful when it leads to a clearer question. Instead of I am just broken, the conversation might become: When feedback is uncertain, I predict rejection, withdraw, and lose the chance to clarify it. That specific sequence gives the work somewhere to begin.

panel.title: A map, not a verdict.
paragraphs: Situation: something happens. Interpretation: you make sense of it. Emotional and physical response: you notice feelings and sensations. Action: you respond, sometimes deliberately and sometimes automatically.
The parts can influence one another. The purpose of mapping them is to create options, not to insist that a distressing event was harmless or that having a thought caused everything that followed.

sections.title: One unanswered message. More than one possible meaning.
sections.intro: Imagine a fictional person whose friend has not replied to an invitation. The example shows a way of examining a pattern, not the correct answer to an actual relationship problem.

items.title: What happened
paragraphs: A day passes without a reply. That is the observable event. The person does not yet know whether the friend is busy, forgot, is unsure about the invitation, or has another reason for not answering.

items.title: What it came to mean
paragraphs: They think: I have upset them; they do not want me around. They feel anxious and embarrassed. They reread previous messages for clues and begin treating their prediction as established information.

items.title: What they do next
paragraphs: They cancel the invitation in a second message and avoid making another. This ends the immediate uncertainty, but also limits the possibility of learning what the friend would have said.

reveal.title: Open a more balanced response to this fictional situation
paragraphs: A more balanced statement could be: I do not know why they have not replied. Rejection is one possible explanation, but I do not have evidence that it is the only one. This is different from insisting, They definitely love me and everything is fine.

A therapist might help the person consider a proportionate follow-up or another manageable response, with attention to the actual relationship and any relevant history. The important shift is separating what is known from what is predicted. There is no instruction here to contact someone who is unsafe or has set a boundary.
The point is not to win an argument against a feeling. It is to see whether a different interpretation and response creates useful information and supports the person's goals.

sections.title: Different tools for different parts of the pattern.
sections.intro: Methods are chosen for the individual formulation and concern. A technique should have an explanation, not just a name.

items.title: Examine an interpretation
items.teaser: Separate an observation from a prediction or conclusion.
paragraphs: A conversation may explore the thought that appeared in a difficult moment, the evidence for it, and information that does not fit it. The alternative is meant to be more accurate or helpful, not artificially cheerful.
For example, a critical comment about one task is not automatically evidence that every part of your work is worthless. It may still identify a real change to make.

items.title: Test a prediction
items.teaser: Use a carefully planned action to learn, rather than only debate.
paragraphs: A behavioral experiment examines a specific prediction. The clinician and client agree what they are trying to learn and how to review the result. This is not the same as performing a task to prove you are brave or compliant.

A fictional example might investigate whether asking a clarifying question always produces the criticism someone predicts. Actual experiments need to fit the person, context, and safety considerations.

items.title: Work with avoidance
items.teaser: Distinguish protection from a pattern that narrows ordinary life.
paragraphs: For some concerns, treatment includes supported steps toward situations that have been avoided. The purpose, pace, and suitability matter. A website cannot establish that a particular situation is safe or prescribe an exposure plan.
Avoiding actual danger is not a failure of therapy. The clinical work needs to distinguish a feared possibility from a genuine risk.

items.title: Build a workable routine
items.teaser: Connect action to what matters, even when motivation is difficult.
paragraphs: Behavioral work may include planning activities or solving practical problems rather than waiting for a change in feeling before doing anything. The plan is adjusted to capacity and circumstances.

A possible discussion is not How do I become productive all the time? but What is one realistic activity that supports connection or a valued part of my life? The activity is a means, not a moral score.

sections.title: A structure that still makes room for you.
sections.intro: This is a general illustration of CBT, not a fixed M.F.T. protocol, an exact session count, or a description of every clinician's appointments.

items.title: Choose a useful focus
paragraphs: You and the clinician identify what needs attention, review relevant changes, and agree what would make the conversation useful. A structure should help keep your priorities visible, not prevent you from raising something important.

items.title: Examine a specific moment
paragraphs: A recent situation can make an abstract concern easier to understand. You look at the meaning it held, the response it brought, and what happened next. The aim is a shared understanding, not a debate the therapist has to win.

items.title: Practice or plan
paragraphs: Depending on the focus, the session may include evaluating a thought, solving a problem, rehearsing a response, or planning a manageable action. The connection between the activity and the goal should be clear.

items.title: Review the learning
paragraphs: You discuss what was useful, what did not fit, and whether there is an agreed practice before the next appointment. Later sessions examine the result and adapt. A worksheet is one possible tool, not the definition of the therapy.

sections.kicker: What CBT is - and is not
sections.title: The method should not erase your circumstances.

items.title: Not: your problems are only in your head.
paragraphs: Real loss, discrimination, illness, financial pressure, or an unsafe relationship cannot be wished away. A useful formulation distinguishes what needs practical change or protection from what can be explored in thinking and behavior.
In the fictional unanswered-message example, having more than one possible explanation does not establish that a relationship is healthy. Context remains part of the question.

items.title: Not: one worksheet fits everyone.
paragraphs: Contemporary CBT emphasizes collaboration and adaptation to a person's background, culture, abilities, experiences, and preferences. Structure and warmth are not opposites. A task that is confusing, inaccessible, or overwhelming needs discussion and adjustment.
You can ask what a technique is for, explain that a description feels inaccurate, or discuss alternatives. The therapeutic relationship is part of the work, not a reward for following instructions.

sections.note: CBT has research support for a range of conditions, but that does not establish the right treatment for a particular person. Assessment, clinician competence for the concern, preferences, and ongoing review all matter.

sections.title: Clinicians whose profiles name CBT.
sections.intro: The cards are generated from the recorded published-profile evidence. Named use is not a claim of a particular certification, expertise in every CBT protocol, or current availability.

sections.title: What the acronym does not tell you.

items.question: Is CBT just positive thinking?
paragraphs: No. The point is not to replace every distressing thought with a reassuring one. In the fictional example above, the balanced response admits uncertainty instead of declaring that nothing is wrong. CBT can examine whether a conclusion fits the evidence and whether a response is helping. It also includes behavior and practical problem solving, not only thoughts.

items.question: Do we ever talk about the past?
paragraphs: CBT commonly focuses on present difficulties and patterns. Relevant earlier experiences can still inform the understanding of a current problem. Present-focused does not mean your history is forbidden; the question is how understanding it helps organize the work you are doing now.

items.question: What happens if I do not complete a task between sessions?
paragraphs: Bring back what got in the way: unclear instructions, time, discomfort, disagreement, or a task that did not fit. That information can help make the next plan more realistic. This is an example of a collaborative conversation, not a promise about one clinician's process. You can ask about expectations before starting.

items.question: How many sessions does CBT take?
paragraphs: There is no single number that applies to every concern and person. Discuss an initial plan, review points, and what would lead to a change. A time-limited approach is not a guarantee that a difficulty will resolve by a particular appointment or a reason to ignore needs that fall outside the original plan.

items.question: Can CBT be used alongside medication or other care?
paragraphs: Psychotherapy can be considered alongside other treatment when appropriate. Medication decisions belong with a qualified prescriber and should take account of your medical situation. This practice page does not offer medication advice or establish that an M.F.T. clinician prescribes. Tell treating providers about the care you are receiving.

items.question: How do I choose a clinician who uses CBT?
paragraphs: Look for a profile that actually names the approach, then ask about the clinician's experience with your concern and the kind of CBT they provide. General familiarity with CBT does not establish training in every specialized protocol. The profiles above are a starting point for that conversation, not a certification directory.
